Talonz51 wrote:
>>Several people have pointed out that CL stop certain decks, like
cryptic mission or corruption decks, cold. And yet certain cards (2nd
trad, 5th trad, deflection, etc.) are excessively powerful and
arguably broken.>>

I'm not quite sure who would argue that Deflection of all cards is broken, but
that is neither here nor there. Assuming that a card is truly broken and
overpowered (and I have no reason to believe that any of the cards you mention
specifically fall under this category), how is limiting the number you play
with going to fix this? When it comes up, it is still broken and overpowered,
and still ruins a game. It just doesn't happen as often, and the game becomes
more of a crap shoot--more random, less strategic.

>>At one time, Jyhad had a list of 'restricted cards', cards that a
player could not have more than X copies of in a deck (it was 6iirc).>>

It was a short time, and was quickly deemed a bad idea. Any problems that the
6CL list was attempting to circumvent were nicely and elegantly fixed by the No
Vote Pushing Rules (which are now simply the official vote rules, and arguably
were the official vote rules when the game was designed--the vote pushing rules
in the original Jyhad rule book were rather ambiguious, and they were turned
into the "dump all you want" rules by a questionable clarification at some
point) and the No Repeat Action rules (used in competetive play). There is no
need for a restricted list with these rules in place. The banned list consists
solely of cards inappropriate for competetive play (ante cards, Madness of the
Bard) and a very few clearly broken (i.e. *way* too powerful) cards that were
simply a bad idea to begin with (Return to Innocence; Monicle of Clarity, which
is a fun and clever card, but perverted by too much logic).

>>Why not do the same now?>>

Because it simply isn't necessary. The game is balanced as it is. A few cards
are probably a tad more powerful than they should be, in terms of cost and
effect, but not many, and they certainly aren't game breaking.

>>Rather than a CL on every card in the game, sliding scale or otherwise, just
restrict the problem cards?>>

'Cause what you seem to think are problem cards simply aren't. The game has a
very rich and varied strategy base. Yes, some strategies are more effective
than others (say weenie Pre bleed when compared to Giovanni Bruise/Bleed), but
the pool of effective strategies is quite large and quite balanced.

I'll have a question / example. As some of you must know by now, I enjoy
playing Lasombra (less than THE, but still...;). THE main combat card in
this Clan is Entombment : no way to reduce damage, good against a For deck.
It is not a hand strike, and must be played close range (no Night of the
Cobra in Obt...). It can be dodged, but no way to use it with IG, so it is
usually either played in defense, or combined with Arms of the Abyss or
Thoughts Betrayed (or Hidden Lurker...).

So, it is very, very tough anyway to use it against a Cel deck, for they
will dodge and addition (and disarm if they have Pot). But it is absolutely
useless against IG.

Now, in CL, a part of the strategy is thinking "he can have only so much of
that card, I already saw him play that many, what are the chances that he'll
still have one in hand ?". This is a little like in some card games, either
like the poker bluff side, or the card-counting there are in other
traditionnal card games. Well, we don't really count, more like evaluate.
Same goes for deflections or CE : sooner or later they'll run out of it, and
when they do, if you have the right hand, they're dead ; so your goal is to
make them discard these, and keep some good cards, well, I won't teach you
how to play this game, you've been at it for longer than me. CL doesn't make
it THAT different.

So I'd like to know what happens in a NCL deck where a Lasombra has chosen
to fight more than a little, and has opted for the Entombment option (not
only, he'll have lots of Pot of course, but we all know that alone it's
usually not enough for a win), and is the predator or prey of a Brujah with
more than 4 IG, not mentionning the dodge / additionals / disarms ??

This is a genuine question, not just an argument.

And concerning the Combat Ends, I can tell you that I've played all those of
PRE (3 x CL) and OBT (2xCL), and that when the enemy has lots of directed
attacks, he can still sometimes get at you. Not easy, but then is it easy in
NCL ? You can always manoeuver (no limit) and than IG is worthless.

So, different limitations, different abuses, but no "broken cards".

Now, if I had ONE suggestion to make about new rules, it wouldn't concern
CL.

I'll post it in another thread, as I think lots of people will (rightly)
avoid any discussion with written CL Vs NCL on it.

Given "poor player" X with some sort of super deck, if he sits at a table with
4 equally bad players with decks of equivelant utility, and he wins, his is a
good player in relation to everyone else there, and deserves to win.

If he sits at a table with 4 other superior players with decks of equal
utility, he is unlikely to win.

Sure, I'll give you that if Poor Player X has a really good deck, and he is
playing against 4 really bad decks, he is likelier to win than not, but if he
is playing against 4 really bad decks, he is either playing against 4 bad
players, at which point we wins by virtue of having better deck
selection/building skills (which makes him a better player than the other 4,
and thus by all rights he should win anyways), or everyone at the table got a
random deck, of which 4 sucked and 1 was good, and he wins by virtue of being
lucky, which happens sometimes in every game.

>>Balance in this context to me would mean that only the best players
with the best decks would win tournaments and/or Championships.>>

And they usually do. I don't dismiss that there is occasionally an anomally--a
generally weak player wins a tournament due to pure luck or whatever, but that
is the case in every competetive game. The people who win large tournaments
filled with solid, well established players? Generally the best players with
the best decks. Ben Peal won the US championships this past summer at Gen Con,
a tournament that had, what, 50-70 players from all over the world. I was in no
way surprised that he won.

>>I find it strange that such a great game would want to be so loppsided in
it's definition of a great player.>>

understands strategy, and can play a table well. All the "great players" I know
fit this defenition.

>>As it stands there are (officially) no great players of this game only great
deck builders that metagamed properly.>>

Metagaming is just as much a part of this game as deckbuilding, and table play.
If you win 'cause you metagamed correctly, this is because you are a good
player. A poor player is incapable of metagaming correctly--if they can do
this, they are a good player.

>>The player has very little tactical role in winning or losing and that is the
last piece of the puzzle as far as I'm concerned.>>

You are mistaken. I often play a Rush deck in competition. My Rush deck is a
good one, and I am a fairly good player (I have been playing a long time, I do
pretty well). I can win tournaments with it. I can say with fair certainty that
if I hand my deck to a random guy who isn't real good, he isn't going anywhere
with it.

Good players make good decks, know how to play them, and know how to play both
the metagame and the table. Not being able to do any of these things makes you
lose. Sure, occasionally you get lucky, but in a grand scheme, the people who
win on a regular basis are the good ones, not the lucky ones.

>>I find this to be the main reason the CL argument comes up so often
the NL'ers are the best deck builders (strategists) and (I may catch

This statement relies on a number of things:

- that there is such a thing, in game terms, as 'excessive'
- that there are 'problem cards'
- that there is 'powermongering' going on

(Also, that there is cheese, but that is a person definition, in most
instances, usually related to decks one personally finds non-challenging
and/or boring.)

A deck, however, that uses multiple copies of a card in large quantities
will find problems:

- generating enough minions to use it
- no repeat actions (NRA, tournament rules)
- no repeat action modifiers (1/minion/action)
- no repeat reactions (1/minion/action)
- generating the circumstances for use (e.g. a 25 Majesty deck that
never gets into combat, and when it does finds that it's being
Immortally Grappled (or whichever anti-S:CE card))
- one dimensionalness (e.g. a deck that ignores politics may be easily
killed by a political predator. I once drew up the third round
seating for GenConUK and was bemused by one of the relationships
drawn up - a Legacy of Pander monster preying on an Obfuscate
stealth-bleed monster)

and so on, in terms of what they will expect to affect them themself.

Then, if a deck is overly overtly powerful it will generate a certain
atmosphere in a tournament or on a table, in that people will often be
disinclined to co-operate with it, and may be inclined to co-operate
with a softer looking grand-predator/prey (say, the actual table
dynamics will vary) - a key facet of a multi-player game.

There is a certain amount of respect for a player who creates such a
deck that rides the metagame, the players, the table dynamics, the decks
s/he sits next to and a little bit of luck too, even if another player
might find it boring.

The best way to deal with so-called problem cards is to deal with them.
If you find a card that you think is overly powerful to a broken extent,
petition the Rules Team (via LSJ) to alter it, with back-up, support,
real life situations, comparative costings etc. Or petition the Design
Team to create hosers for it (e.g. Telepathic Tracking's creation is, in
part, a response to many complaints about the relative power of S:CE).
